newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. said tried to overlook Samper drug smear.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said tried to overlook Samper drug smear.

text.p: The United States struck a tentative deal with Colombia's president-elect Ernesto Samper in 1994 to turn a blind eye to evidence that he funded his election campaign with drug money, a former state department official said on Thursday.

But Washington, apparently fearing political embarassment, welched on the deal when the scandal of Samper's alleged ties to drug kingpins became increasingly public after he took office, Michael Skol, a former first assistant secretary of state, said.

"It's true that the U.S. government, myself and (Assistant U.S. Secretary of State Robert) Gelbard talked with candidate and president-elect Samper about the suspicions and evidence that his campaign had accepted cartel money," Skol told a news conference in Bogota.

"It's also true that at that moment the most important thing was not the past but the present and the future," he added, declining to comment in more detail on the exact content of the conversations saying such information was still classified.
Samper was accused of knowingly accepting $6 million dollars in cocaine cash from the powerful Cali cartel to fund his presidential election run.

An inquiry by Congress, dominated by Samper's ruling Liberal Party, cleared him of any blame. But the United States refused to accept that decision and only last month Gelbard -- whom Skol said was one of the ones who initially agreed to overlook Samper's murky past -- called the inquiry that acquitted him a "patently flawed process."
Washington last week blacklisted Colombia for a second consecutive year for failure to do enough to combat drug-trafficking.
